title: Design Considerations for Faster-Than-Light (FTL) Communication
summary: This is a humorous April 1st RFC. It imagines communication faster than light and reasons that packets would then arrive before they are sent. It jokes about what that would mean for the design of Internet protocols. It is satire, not a real specification.

plainLanguage.summary: This joke imagines messages so fast they arrive before you send them, like getting a reply before asking the question, and wonders what a mess that would make.

questions: packets arriving before they are sent
subtitle: An April 1st exploration of internet protocols for faster-than-light communication.

tldr.problem: This is a joke RFC from April 1, 2013. It takes physics seriously and imagines what would happen if internet protocols had to work with communication faster than light.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC explains that faster-than-light communication would reverse time, meaning packets arrive before they are sent, breaking assumptions in protocols like TCP.
tldr.outcome: The joke explores how protocols would need redesign, with tongue-in-cheek seriousness about negative round-trip times, reverse causality, and the problems that would create.

today: RFC 6921 is an Informational RFC published as a joke on April 1, 2013. It has not been obsoleted and remains a lighthearted exploration of what would happen if the impossible physics of faster-than-light communication suddenly became real.

sections.title: Faster-Than-Light Communication (April 1st RFC)
sections.content:
RFC 6921 is a humorous April Fools' document from April 1, 2013. It is not a serious proposal, but rather a joke that takes an impossible premise and explores it with academic rigor.

The premise is playful physics: as we approach the speed of light, time slows down. So logically, if we go faster than light, time would reverse. The consequence for the internet would be profound: packets would arrive before they were sent. This creates a cascade of absurd protocol problems that the RFC explores with straight-faced seriousness.
sections.plainLanguage: On April 1st, 2013, someone joked about what would happen if the internet was so fast packets arrived before you sent them. It would break everything.

sections.title: The Protocol Problem
sections.content:
Today's internet protocols, including the fundamental TCP (Transmission Control Protocol), assume that a sender transmits a packet before the receiver gets it. That basic assumption collapses in a faster-than-light world.

The RFC walks through TCP's three-way handshake—the dance two endpoints perform to establish a connection—and shows how it breaks when packets arrive in reverse order. With FTL communication, the receiver would see the first SYN packet before the sender even creates it. The author notes, with unexpected optimism, that TCP's symmetrical design might actually handle this by accident, as long as the processing time is larger than the backwards time shift.

Other problems emerge: congestion control algorithms that divide by round-trip time would face negative RTT values. Networks would theoretically be able to prevent congestion before it starts. The RFC humbles readers with the idea that TCP's designers showed "remarkable forethought" in creating something that might work in this impossible scenario.
sections.plainLanguage: Talking to another computer normally goes: you send, then they receive. With FTL, they receive before you send. The rules of internet conversations would all be backwards.

sections.title: Recommendations and Security
sections.content:
The RFC earnestly recommends that the IETF create a review group to check all new protocols for FTL compatibility. It suggests auditing every existing protocol to ensure they work when packets arrive before they're sent. For security, it notes that exploits would thrive in an FTL world, and hints darkly that malware authors might already be taking advantage of these properties.

The whole document maintains a tone of mock-serious analysis, treating an impossible physics scenario as though it were an engineering challenge just around the corner.
sections.plainLanguage: The joke ends with the author seriously suggesting the internet should prepare for this, as if it's really going to happen.
